markingScheme.criterion: Quotes at least two of the student's own logged Neutralisation Station readings (an amount of alkali added with its pH, e.g. pH 1 at 0 mL and pH 7 near 25 mL for stomach acid) as evidence.
markingScheme.accept: Any two genuine volume/pH pairs from the student's own Investigation Record rows; exact wording not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: A general claim ('the pH goes up') with no actual logged readings quoted.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains neutralisation: the alkali (base) reacts with the acid and cancels it out, so the pH rises toward 7 and the liquid becomes neutral (green indicator).
markingScheme.accept: Any valid phrasing that an acid and a base react/cancel so the solution becomes less acidic and reaches pH 7.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying only 'the pH changed' or 'it got neutral' with no mention of the acid and base reacting or cancelling.

markingScheme.criterion: States that adding too much alkali made the pH go above 7 so the liquid became a base (alkaline), shown by a blue or purple indicator - the acid had all been used up.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that overshooting makes the mixture alkaline/basic with pH above 7.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying only 'it went wrong' or giving no direction or pH for the overshoot.

markingScheme.criterion: Identifies that the antacid tablet is the better choice because it contains a base (pH above 7) that neutralises the stomach acid and raises the pH toward 7.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that the antacid is a base which neutralises the acid.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'the antacid is better' with no reason.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that lemon juice is itself an acid (pH about 2), so it would add more acid and make things worse rather than neutralising.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that lemon juice is acidic so would not neutralise stomach acid.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying lemon juice is 'bad for you' with no reference to it being an acid.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains why sodium hydroxide would not be safe: it is a very strong, corrosive base (pH about 13), so it would burn and could overshoot far past neutral; a safe choice is a weak base in a small, controlled amount.
markingScheme.accept: Any valid reference to a strong base being corrosive/dangerous or overshooting neutral.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying only 'it is a chemical' or 'it is bad' with no reference to strength, corrosiveness or overshooting.
